case.case_title: M. N. D. Perera vs Balapatabendi, Secretary to the President and others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. (F.R.) No. 27/2002, decided on 8 September 2004

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was unlawfully excluded from attending and covering the swearing-in ceremony of the Prime Minister at the President's House, thereby violating his right to equality before the law and equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that his exclusion from the President’s House to cover the swearing-in ceremony was discriminatory and violated his fundamental rights under Article 12(1), 12(2), and 14(1)(a) of the Constitution.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the swearing-in was not a public function, the President’s House is not a public place, and the petitioner was not treated unequally as access was by invitation only and no right of access existed for the petitioner.
key_facts: The petitioner was the News Editor of TNL and sought to cover the swearing-in of the Prime Minister on 9 December 2001.
The petitioner and his crew were body searched and identified but were denied entry by Presidential Security Division on the President’s instruction.
Other media personnel were allowed to cover the event.
The petitioner had no invitation to enter the President’s House.
The President’s House is the official residence and not a public place accessible to the general public.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the law, which prohibits arbitrary and discriminatory exclusion. The swearing-in ceremony was a public function held at the President’s House, which, although an official residence, includes areas used for public functions. Excluding the petitioner without valid security or logistical reasons constituted unlawful discrimination violating Article 12(1).
reasoning.application_to_facts: The petitioner was singled out and excluded from the event despite following all security procedures and other media being allowed. The President’s House was deemed a venue for a public function, and the exclusion was based on political opinion or personal animosity, which is impermissible under Article 12(1).
principles_established: Equality before the law includes protection against arbitrary exclusion from public functions.
Official residences may host public functions where constitutional rights apply.
Discrimination based on political opinion or personal animosity violates Article 12(1).
Directives from the President cannot justify manifestly illegal discrimination.
precedents_cited: Bernard Soysa and Others v AG (1991) Sri LR 56
Victor Ivan v Silva (1998) 1 Sri LR 340
Visuvalingam and Others vs Liyanage and Others No (1) (1983) 1 Sri LR 203
Wijesuriya v The State IT NLR 25
Sunila Abeysekera v Ariya Rubasinghe Competent Authority and Others (2000) 1 Sri LR 314

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioner’s exclusion violated his right to equality before the law and equal protection under Article 12(1). The exclusion was unlawful and discriminatory.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The petitioner was awarded Rs. 5,000 as compensation and Rs. 2,500 as costs payable by the State.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court’s reasoning as it protects against arbitrary and discriminatory treatment by the State. The petitioner’s exclusion from a public function without valid reason was found to violate this clause, leading to the court’s decision to grant relief.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner and his crew were denied entry to the President’s House on the President’s instruction despite following security procedures, while other media were allowed, constituting unlawful discrimination violating Article 12(1).
